claim: Pupil size is a well-established marker of effort.
source: Pupil size is an established marker of effort (Kahneman, 1973; Bumke, 1911; Laeng et al., 2012; Mathôt, 2018; Strauch et al., 2022; Loewenfeld, 1993; Sirois and Brisson, 2014; van der Wel and van Steenbergen, 2018; Beatty, 1982).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing pupil size as an effort marker.

claim: Pupil size reflects the effort associated with making a saccade ('saccade costs').
source: We recently showed that pupil size, a well-established marker of effort, also reflects the effort associated with making a saccade ('saccade costs').
evidence: Authors reference their own recent work demonstrating this relationship.

claim: When choosing between two saccade directions, the least costly direction was consistently preferred.
source: Here, we demonstrate saccade costs to critically drive saccade selection: when choosing between any two saccade directions, the least costly direction was consistently preferred.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The principle that least costly saccade directions are preferred holds during search in natural scenes.
source: Strikingly, this principle even held during search in natural scenes in two additional experiments.
evidence: Supported by data from two additional experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing cognitive demand through an auditory counting task causes participants to make fewer saccades.
source: When increasing cognitive demand experimentally through an auditory counting task, participants made fewer saccades and especially cut costly directions.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the dual-task manipulation in the study.

claim: Under increased cognitive demand, participants especially cut costly saccade directions.
source: When increasing cognitive demand experimentally through an auditory counting task, participants made fewer saccades and especially cut costly directions.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the dual-task manipulation in the study.

claim: The eye-movement system and other cognitive operations consume similar resources that are flexibly allocated among each other as cognitive demand changes.
source: This suggests that the eye-movement system and other cognitive operations consume similar resources that are flexibly allocated among each other as cognitive demand changes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dual-task experimental results.

claim: Eye-movement behavior is tuned to adaptively minimize saccade-inherent effort.
source: Together, we argue that eye-movement behavior is tuned to adaptively minimize saccade-inherent effort.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion drawn from all experimental findings.

claim: Saccades are executed approximately three to four times per second.
source: Saccades are executed approximately three to four times per second (Henderson, 2003; Henderson and Hollingworth, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade frequency.

claim: Where to saccade is one of the most frequent decisions the brain is faced with.
source: Where to saccade is, therefore, one of the most frequent decisions the brain is faced with (Bargary et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on saccade frequency, supported by citation.

claim: Physical properties of the environment (bottom-up information) drive where the eyes are moved.
source: It is well established that the physical properties of the environment (bottom-up information) (Kümmerer et al., 2022; Kümmerer et al., 2016; Itti et al., 1998; Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 1994), the goals of the observer (top-down information) (Posner, 1980; Petersen and Posner, 2012; Posner and Petersen, 1990; Desimone and Duncan, 1995), and prior knowledge about a scene (selection history) (Awh et al., 2012; Theeuwes et al., 2022) drive where the eyes are moved.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established research.

claim: The goals of the observer (top-down information) drive where the eyes are moved.
source: It is well established that the physical properties of the environment (bottom-up information) (Kümmerer et al., 2022; Kümmerer et al., 2016; Itti et al., 1998; Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 1994), the goals of the observer (top-down information) (Posner, 1980; Petersen and Posner, 2012; Posner and Petersen, 1990; Desimone and Duncan, 1995), and prior knowledge about a scene (selection history) (Awh et al., 2012; Theeuwes et al., 2022) drive where the eyes are moved.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established research.

claim: Prior knowledge about a scene (selection history) drives where the eyes are moved.
source: It is well established that the physical properties of the environment (bottom-up information) (Kümmerer et al., 2022; Kümmerer et al., 2016; Itti et al., 1998; Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 1994), the goals of the observer (top-down information) (Posner, 1980; Petersen and Posner, 2012; Posner and Petersen, 1990; Desimone and Duncan, 1995), and prior knowledge about a scene (selection history) (Awh et al., 2012; Theeuwes et al., 2022) drive where the eyes are moved.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established research.

claim: There is a bias for cardinal compared with oblique saccade directions.
source: However, even when these factors are kept constant, there are many systematic biases in eye-movement behavior, such as a bias for cardinal compared with oblique saccade directions (Foulsham and Kingstone, 2010; Gilchrist and Harvey, 2006; Bays and Husain, 2012; Anderson et al., 2008; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003; Tatler and Vincent, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research documenting this bias.

claim: The presence of systematic biases in eye-movement behavior suggests that additional factors must contribute to saccade selection.
source: The presence of these biases suggests that additional factors must contribute to the decision of where to saccade, here referred to as 'saccade selection.'
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation of unexplained biases.

claim: The effort involved with planning and executing movements may be a crucial factor in driving action selection.
source: Recent evidence suggests that the effort involved with planning and executing (eye) movements may be one crucial factor in driving action selection (Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020; Thomas et al., 2022; Hagura et al., 2017; Kadner et al., 2022; Cos et al., 2014; Cos et al., 2011; Cos et al., 2012; Todorov and Jordan, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research on effort and action selection.

claim: Effort is thought to be minimized whenever possible.
source: Effort is thought to be minimized whenever possible (Hull, 1943; Tsai, 1932), likely because it is costly to spend inherently limited cognitive resources (Friston, 2010; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on effort minimization.

claim: It is costly to spend inherently limited cognitive resources.
source: Effort is thought to be minimized whenever possible (Hull, 1943; Tsai, 1932), likely because it is costly to spend inherently limited cognitive resources (Friston, 2010; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on cognitive resources.

claim: Saccades are relatively affordable (not very costly).
source: Although saccades are relatively affordable [i.e. not very costly; Findlay and Gilchrist, 2003; Theeuwes, 2012], they are executed very often (Henderson, 2003; Henderson and Hollingworth, 1998) and, therefore, even small costs should add up over time (Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020; Koevoet et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade costs.

claim: Even small saccade costs should add up over time because saccades are executed very often.
source: Although saccades are relatively affordable [i.e. not very costly; Findlay and Gilchrist, 2003; Theeuwes, 2012], they are executed very often (Henderson, 2003; Henderson and Hollingworth, 1998) and, therefore, even small costs should add up over time (Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020; Koevoet et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on saccade frequency and cost accumulation, supported by citations.

claim: Computational models suggest that saccade costs predict saccade behavior.
source: This would be in line with recent evidence from computational models suggesting that saccade costs predict saccade behavior [e.g. Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2019; Kadner et al., 2022; Thomas et al., 2022].
evidence: Supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claim: Previous studies either assumed saccade costs or indirectly inferred them from gaze behavior itself.
source: These studies either assumed saccade costs or indirectly inferred them from gaze behavior itself.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research methods in the field.

claim: No study has been able to quantify saccade costs (neuro-)physiologically until recently.
source: However, no study has been able to quantify saccade costs (neuro-)physiologically, and therefore been able to directly test this hypothesis until recently.
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the field prior to recent work.

claim: The effort of saccade planning can be measured with pupil size when low-level visual factors are controlled for.
source: We recently demonstrated that the effort of saccade planning can be measured with pupil size, which allows for a physiological quantification of saccade costs as long as low-level visual factors are controlled for (Koevoet et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, cited here.

claim: Loading more in working memory results in stronger pupil dilation.
source: For instance, loading more in working memory or tracking more objects results in stronger pupil dilation (Beatty, 1982; Koevoet et al., 2024; Robison and Unsworth, 2019; Alnæs et al., 2014; Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Unsworth and Miller, 2021; Unsworth and Robison, 2015; Ahern and Beatty, 1979; Hess and Polt, 1964).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on pupil dilation and working memory.

claim: Tracking more objects results in stronger pupil dilation.
source: For instance, loading more in working memory or tracking more objects results in stronger pupil dilation (Beatty, 1982; Koevoet et al., 2024; Robison and Unsworth, 2019; Alnæs et al., 2014; Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Unsworth and Miller, 2021; Unsworth and Robison, 2015; Ahern and Beatty, 1979; Hess and Polt, 1964).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on pupil dilation and object tracking.

claim: Pupil size reflects not only cognitive effort but also the effort of planning and executing movements.
source: Pupil size not only reflects cognitive (or mental) effort but also the effort of planning and executing movements (Naber and Murphy, 2020; Richer and Beatty, 1985; Bumke, 1911).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on pupil size and movement effort.

claim: Saccade costs are higher for oblique compared with cardinal directions.
source: We leveraged this to demonstrate that saccade costs can be captured with pupil size, and are higher for oblique compared with cardinal directions (Koevoet et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, cited here.

claim: Pupil size differed across saccade directions during saccade planning.
source: Replicating our previous findings, we found that pupil size differed across directions (Koevoet et al., 2023; Figure 1c–f).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, shown in Figure 1c-f.

claim: Pupil size during planning of oblique saccades was larger compared with cardinal saccades.
source: We observed a larger pupil size during planning of oblique saccades compared with cardinal saccades (β = 7.662, SE  = 1.957, t = 3.916, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study's data analysis.

claim: Downward saccades were associated with a larger pupil size than upward saccades.
source: Downward saccades were associated with a larger pupil size than upward saccades (β = 0.556, SE  = 0.171, t = 3.261, p = 0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study's data analysis.

claim: Pupil size was slightly larger for leftward compared with rightward saccades.
source: and we found a slightly larger pupil size for leftward compared with rightward saccades (β = 0.226, SE  = 0.095, t = 2.388, p = 0.017).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study's data analysis.

claim: The effects of saccade direction on pupil size were not mediated by differences in saccade properties such as duration, amplitude, peak velocity, and landing precision.
source: These effects were not mediated by differences in saccade properties, such as duration, amplitude, peak velocity, and landing precision (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study's statistical analysis, shown in Figure 1e and f.

claim: Saccade costs differ as a function of direction.
source: Together, this shows that saccade costs differ as a function of direction, indicating that certain saccades are more costly than others.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pupil size data across directions.

claim: Participants preferred cardinal over oblique saccade directions.
source: Results showed that participants preferred cardinal over oblique directions (β = 0.091, SE = 0.023, t = 3.910, p < 0.001; Figure 2b)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade preference task, shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Participants preferred upward over downward saccade directions.
source: and preferred upward over downward directions (β = 0.036, SE = 0.017, t = 2.130, p = 0.033).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade preference task.

claim: No differences were observed between leftward and rightward saccade directions in preferences.
source: No differences were observed between leftward and rightward saccade directions (β = 0.009, SE = 0.014, t = 0.668, p = 0.504).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade preference task.

claim: Pupil size during saccade planning negatively correlated with saccade preferences.
source: In line with our hypothesis, pupil size during saccade planning (in cued directions) negatively correlated with saccade preferences (during self-selection) (r(34) = –0.76, p < 0.001; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlating the two tasks, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Intrinsic saccade costs critically predict saccade preferences.
source: For the first time, this demonstrates that intrinsic saccade costs critically predict saccade preferences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between pupil size and preferences.

claim: Participants preferred saccading towards affordable over costly options.
source: Put differently, participants preferred saccading towards affordable over costly options.
evidence: This is a restatement of the main finding from the preference task.

claim: The correlation between pupil size and saccade preferences was not driven by other oculomotor metrics such as saccade latency and landing precision.
source: A control analysis ruled out that the correlation between pupil size and saccade preferences was driven by other oculomotor metrics such as saccade latency and landing precision (see Supporting Information).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Pupil sizes during saccade planning were smaller for preferred directions than for avoided directions.
source: Illustrating the robustness of this relationship further, we found smaller pupil sizes during saccade planning for preferred (selected >50%) than for avoided (selected <50%) directions (t(19) = 4.38, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.979; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing preferred vs avoided directions, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Saccade costs predicted saccade selection on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: As another test of the robustness of the effect, we analyzed whether saccade costs predicted saccade selection on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This is a finding from a trial-by-trial analysis in the study.

claim: The more affordable option was chosen above chance level (56.64%) across participants.
source: Complementing the above analyses, the more affordable option was chosen above chance level across participants (M = 56.64%, 95% CI = [52.75–60.52%], one-sample t-test against 50%: t(19) = 3.26, p = 0.004, Cohen's d = 0.729; Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the trial-by-trial analysis, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Saccade costs robustly predict saccade preferences.
source: Together, these analyses established that saccade costs robustly predict saccade preferences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple converging analyses.

claim: Saccade curvature reflects conflict between target and distractor saccade vectors.
source: Saccade curvature reflects conflict between target and distractor saccade vectors: if a distractor is inhibited, and the target is activated, the saccade curves away from the distractor location (Van der Stigchel et al., 2006; McPeek et al., 2003; Van der Stigchel, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade curvature.

claim: When saccade costs differ more between directions, there should be more conflict between saccade vectors.
source: Whenever saccade costs differ more between directions, there should, therefore, be more conflict between saccade vectors.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the relationship between cost differences and conflict.

claim: If both saccade directions were equally costly, there would be no need for conflict as cost minimization is impossible.
source: If both directions were equally costly, there would be no need for conflict as cost minimization is impossible.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between cost differences and conflict.

claim: Weighing costs and reward in decision-making takes time.
source: Furthermore, weighing costs (and reward) in decision-making is known to take time (Spering, 2022, Polanía et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on decision-making time.

claim: More elaborate decisions should show in more curvature and longer saccade latencies.
source: More elaborate decisions should, therefore, not only show in more curvature, but also in longer saccade latencies.
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from the relationship between decision complexity and oculomotor properties.

claim: Saccades curved away from the non-selected option in the majority of trials (78.15%).
source: Saccades curved away from the non-selected option in the majority of trials, indicating oculomotor conflict (Figure 3a; M = 78.15%, 95% CI = [74.734–81.567%], t(19) = 15.741, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 3.519).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the saccade curvature analysis, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: When the difference in pupil size between two saccade options was larger, saccades curved away more from the non-selected option.
source: Whenever the difference in pupil size between the two options was larger, saccades curved away more from the non-selected option (β = 0.004, SE  = 0.001, t = 4.448, p < 0.001; Figure 3b)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of curvature and cost differences, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: When the difference in pupil size between two saccade options was larger, saccade latencies slowed.
source: and their latencies slowed (β = 0.050, SE  = 0.013, t = 4.323, p < 0.001; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of latency and cost differences, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Cost is actively weighed during saccade selection and leads to stronger conflict when cost differences are larger.
source: Our results show that cost is actively weighed and leads to stronger conflict whenever cost differences are larger.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the curvature and latency findings.

claim: More elaborate decisions in saccade selection are predominantly made when warranted by sufficient differences in saccade costs between options.
source: This suggests that more elaborate decisions in saccade selection are predominantly made when warranted by sufficient differences in saccade costs between options.
evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between cost differences and decision complexity.

claim: Pupil size predicted saccade selection above chance (59.72%) when saccades curved away from the non-selected option.
source: Pupil size (i.e. saccade cost) predicted saccade selection when saccades curved away (M = 59.72%, 95% CI = [55.208–64.233%], t(19) = 4.116, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.920)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the trial-by-trial analysis split by curvature direction.

claim: Pupil size did not predict saccade selection when saccades curved toward the non-selected option.
source: but not toward (M = 48.42%, 95% CI = [44.496–52.338%], t(19) = 0.771, P = 0.450, Cohen's d = 0.172) the non-selected option.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the trial-by-trial analysis split by curvature direction.

claim: Prediction accuracies differed between toward and away curving saccades.
source: These prediction accuracies differed between curve directions (t(19) = 4.795, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.072; Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing prediction accuracies, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Saccade costs were predominantly considered when saccades curved away from the non-selected option.
source: This shows that saccade costs were predominantly considered when saccades curved away.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential prediction accuracies.

claim: The costs of potential saccade targets are especially weighed during saccade selection when warranted by large differences in saccade costs.
source: Together, these analyses suggest that the costs of potential saccade targets are especially weighed during saccade selection when warranted by large differences in saccade costs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the curvature and prediction accuracy analyses.

claim: When cost differences are large, oculomotor conflict increases and saccade cost plays a bigger role in saccade selection.
source: In these cases, oculomotor conflict increases and saccade cost plays a bigger role in saccade selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the relationship between cost differences, conflict, and selection.

claim: A negative relationship was observed between pupil size and saccade preferences in Experiment 1 of natural viewing.
source: As hypothesized, we observed a negative relationship between pupil size and saccade preferences in both experiments (Exp. 1: β = 1.784, SE  = 0.324, t = 5.412, p < 0.001; saccade preferences in Figure 4b, link in Figure 4c
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the natural viewing data analysis, shown in Figures 4b and 4c.

claim: A negative relationship was observed between pupil size and saccade preferences in Experiment 2 of natural viewing.
source: Exp. 2: β = 0.644, SE  = 0.170, t = 3.780, p < 0.001; saccade preferences in Figure 4d, link in Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the natural viewing data analysis, shown in Figures 4d and 4e.

claim: Even when participants made unconstrained eye movements in natural scenes, saccade cost remained linked to saccade preferences.
source: This shows that even when participants made unconstrained eye movements in natural scenes, saccade cost remained linked to saccade preferences: affordable directions were preferred over costly directions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the natural viewing experiments.

claim: The additional cognitive demand of the dual task led to a decreased saccade frequency.
source: The additional cognitive demand of the dual task indeed led to a decreased saccade frequency (t(24) = 7.224, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.445; Figure 4h).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the dual-task manipulation, shown in Figure 4h.

claim: The auditory dual task and the oculomotor system, at least in part, consumed from a shared pool of cognitive resources.
source: This indicates that the auditory dual task and the oculomotor system, at least in part, consumed from a shared pool of cognitive resources.
evidence: This is an inference from the decreased saccade frequency under dual-task conditions.

claim: Pupil size negatively linked with the saccade adjustment map between single and dual tasks.
source: Nevertheless, pupil size negatively linked with the adjustment map as hypothesized (β = 9.333, SE  = 0.966, t = 9.659, p < 0.001; Figure 4i; while controlling for the same possible covariates as before).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the adjustment analysis, shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Costly saccades were cut disproportionally when more cognitive resources were consumed by the additional auditory dual task.
source: This shows that costly saccades were cut disproportionally when more cognitive resources were consumed by the additional auditory dual task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the negative relationship between pupil size and adjustment.

claim: Cognitive resources are flexibly (dis)allocated from and to the oculomotor system based on the current resource demands.
source: This demonstrates that cognitive resources are flexibly (dis)allocated from and to the oculomotor system based on the current resource demands.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dual-task findings.

claim: Affordable saccades were preferred over costly ones.
source: We observed that affordable saccades were preferred over costly ones.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the preference task.

claim: When two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, higher oculomotor conflict was found as indexed by stronger saccade trajectory deviations away from the non-selected option.
source: Furthermore, when two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, we found higher oculomotor conflict as indexed by stronger saccade trajectory deviations away from the non-selected option and increased onset latencies.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the curvature and latency analyses.

claim: When two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, increased onset latencies were found.
source: Furthermore, when two possible saccade directions differed more in saccade cost, we found higher oculomotor conflict as indexed by stronger saccade trajectory deviations away from the non-selected option and increased onset latencies.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the curvature and latency analyses.

claim: Saccade directions were flexibly adjusted based on cost as cognitive demand increased.
source: Lastly, saccade directions were flexibly adjusted based on cost as cognitive demand increased.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the dual-task experiment.

claim: Saccade costs fundamentally underlie saccade selection, even when physical salience, the goals of the observer, and selection history affect where the eyes are moved.
source: Together, this demonstrates that saccade costs fundamentally underlie saccade selection, even when physical salience, the goals of the observer, and selection history affect where the eyes are moved.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experiments in the study.

claim: At least three processes contribute to the total cost of a saccade: the complexity of oculomotor programming, shifting of presaccadic attention, and predictive/spatial remapping.
source: We speculate that at least three processes contribute to the total cost of a saccade (Koevoet et al., 2023): the complexity of oculomotor programming (Jainta et al., 2011; Wang and Munoz, 2021; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020), shifting of presaccadic attention (Rizzolatti et al., 1987; Deubel and Schneider, 1996), and predictive/spatial remapping (Rolfs, 2015; Melcher, 2007; Bays and Husain, 2007; Fabius et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Oblique but not cardinal saccades require communication between pontine and midbrain circuits.
source: For example, oblique but not cardinal saccades require communication between pontine and midbrain circuits (Sparks, 2002; King and Fuchs, 1979; Curthoys et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade neural circuitry.

claim: Differences in neural complexity may underlie the additional costs of oblique compared with cardinal saccades.
source: Such differences in neural complexity may underlie the additional costs of oblique compared with cardinal saccades.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the neural basis of saccade costs.

claim: Presaccadic attention is shifted prior to each saccade to prepare the brain for the abrupt changes in retinal input resulting from saccades through spatial/predictive remapping.
source: Furthermore, presaccadic attention is shifted prior to each saccade to prepare the brain for the abrupt changes in retinal input resulting from saccades through spatial/predictive remapping (Melcher and Colby, 2008; Rolfs, 2015; Melcher, 2007; Bays and Husain, 2007; Rizzolatti et al., 1987; Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Van der Stigchel and Hollingworth, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on presaccadic attention and remapping.

claim: Preparation for upcoming changes in retinal input consumes neurocognitive resources and likely contributes to saccade costs.
source: This preparation for upcoming changes in retinal input consumes neurocognitive resources and, therefore, likely also contributes to saccade costs (Koevoet et al., 2023; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations.

claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in perception.
source: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in perception (Wexler et al., 2022; Barbot et al., 2021; Baldwin et al., 2012; Greenwood et al., 2017; Chakravarthi et al., 2022; Abrams et al., 2012; Ezzo et al., 2023)
evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in attention.
source: attention (Hanning et al., 2024; Hanning et al., 2022; Schütz, 2014; Carrasco et al., 2001; Mackeben, 1999; Ohl et al., 2024)
evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in saccade characteristics.
source: saccade characteristics (Hanning et al., 2024; Greenwood et al., 2017; Hanning et al., 2022; Ohl et al., 2024)
evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The observed differences in saccade costs across directions could be linked to established anisotropies in (early) visual cortex.
source: and (early) visual cortex (Himmelberg et al., 2022; Van Essen et al., 1984; Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2018; also see Himmelberg et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research, supported by citations.

claim: The upper visual field is relatively underrepresented in early visual areas.
source: For example, downward saccades are more costly than upward saccades, which mimics a similar asymmetry in early visual areas wherein the upper visual field is relatively underrepresented (Himmelberg et al., 2022; Van Essen et al., 1984; Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on visual field representation.

claim: Stronger presaccadic benefits are found for down- compared with upward saccades.
source: similarly stronger presaccadic benefits are found for down- compared with upward saccades (Hanning et al., 2024, Hanning et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on presaccadic attention.

claim: Upward saccades are more precise than downward saccades.
source: Moreover, upward saccades are more precise than downward saccades (Greenwood et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on saccade precision.

claim: Saccade latency has been proposed to index oculomotor effort.
source: For example, saccade latency has been proposed to index oculomotor effort (Shadmehr et al., 2019), whereby saccades with longer latencies are associated with more oculomotor effort.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on saccade latency and effort.

claim: Saccade latency is a possible complementary marker of saccade costs.
source: This makes saccade latency a possible complementary marker of saccade costs (also see Appendix).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about alternative measures of saccade cost.

claim: Pupil size allows capturing not only the costs of saccades, but also of covert attentional shifts.
source: Pupil size, therefore, allows to capture not only the costs of saccades, but also of covert attentional shifts (Koevoet et al., 2023), or shifts with other effectors such as head or arm movements (Richer and Beatty, 1985; Voudouris et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on pupil size and various types of movements.

claim: Pupil size can measure saccade costs even when searching in natural scenes.
source: Second, as we have demonstrated, pupil size can measure saccade costs even when searching in natural scenes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural viewing experiments, shown in Figure 4.

claim: During natural viewing, it is difficult to disentangle fixation duration from saccade latencies.
source: During natural viewing, it is difficult to disentangle fixation duration from saccade latencies, complicating the use of saccade latency as a measure of saccade cost.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about measuring saccade latency in natural viewing.

claim: The findings are in line with established effort-based models that assume costs to be weighed against rewards during decision-making.
source: Our findings are in line with established effort-based models that assume costs to be weighed against rewards during decision-making (Kool et al., 2010; Kurzban et al., 2013; Shenhav et al., 2021; Shenhav et al., 2013; Shenhav et al., 2017; Westbrook and Braver, 2015).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: The intrinsic costs of arm movements are considered during decision-making: biomechanically affordable movements are generally preferred over more costly ones.
source: Relatedly, the intrinsic costs of arm movements are also considered during decision-making: biomechanically affordable movements are generally preferred over more costly ones (Cos et al., 2011; Cos et al., 2014; Cos et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on arm movement costs.

claim: Until now, the intrinsic costs of saccades and other movements have been inferred from gaze behavior itself or by using computational modeling.
source: First, until now, the intrinsic costs of saccades and other movements have been inferred from gaze behavior itself or by using computational modeling (Thomas et al., 2022; Kadner et al., 2022; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2019; Cos et al., 2011; Cos et al., 2014; Cos et al., 2012; Petitet et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research methods, supported by citations.

claim: The current study directly measured cost physiologically using pupil size.
source: In contrast, we directly measured cost physiologically using pupil size.
evidence: This is a methodological contribution of the current study.

claim: Physiologically measured saccade costs predict where saccades are directed in a controlled binary preference task and during natural viewing.
source: Second, we show that physiologically measured saccade costs predict where saccades are directed in a controlled binary preference task, and even during natural viewing.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from both the preference task and natural viewing experiments.

claim: Cost-based decision-making may be a general property of the brain.
source: However, cost-based decision-making may be a more general property of the brain (Friston, 2010; Kahneman, 1973; Attneave, 1959; Hasenstaub et al., 2010; Jamadar et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the generality of cost-based decision-making, supported by citations.

claim: Every action, be it physical or cognitive, is associated with an intrinsic cost.
source: Every action, be it physical or cognitive, is associated with an intrinsic cost, and pupil size is likely a general marker of this (Beatty, 1982).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the generality of action costs, supported by citation.

claim: Pupil dilation does not always reflect cost, as the pupil dilates in response to many sensory and cognitive factors.
source: Note, however, that pupil dilation does not always reflect cost, as the pupil dilates in response to many sensory and cognitive factors which should be controlled for, or at least considered, when interpreting pupillometric data [e.g., see Mathôt and Vilotijević, 2023; Strauch et al., 2022; Mathôt, 2018; Sirois and Brisson, 2014].
evidence: This is a methodological caveat about interpreting pupil size, supported by citations.

claim: Effort-linked pupil dilations are thought to be, at least in part, driven by activity in the brainstem locus coeruleus (LC).
source: Effort-linked pupil dilations are thought to be, at least in part, driven by activity in the brainstem locus coeruleus (LC) (Joshi et al., 2016; Joshi and Gold, 2020; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005b; Strauch et al., 2022) [but other neurotransmitters also affect pupil size, e.g. Grujic et al., 2024, Mazancieux et al., 2023].
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on the neural basis of pupil dilation.

claim: Activity in LC is considered to be crucial for the communication within and between neural populations and modulates global neural gain.
source: Activity in LC with its widespread connections throughout the brain (Schwarz and Luo, 2015; Szabadi, 2013; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005b; Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003; Aston-Jones and Waterhouse, 2016; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005a) is considered to be crucial for the communication within and between neural populations and modulates global neural gain (Poe et al., 2020; Wainstein et al., 2022; Dahl et al., 2022; Corbetta et al., 2008; Posner et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on LC function.

claim: Neural firing is costly.
source: Neural firing is costly (Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020; Attwell and Laughlin, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on the metabolic cost of neural activity.

claim: LC activity and pupil size are (neuro)physiologically plausible markers of cost.
source: and therefore LC activity and pupil size are (neuro)physiologically plausible markers of cost (Strauch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference about the validity of pupil size as a cost marker, supported by citation.

claim: Continued exertion of effort (accompanied by altered pupil dilation) is linked to the accumulation of glutamate in the lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Tentative evidence even suggests that continued exertion of effort (accompanied by altered pupil dilation) is linked to the accumulation of glutamate in the lateral prefrontal cortex (Wiehler et al., 2022), which may be a metabolic marker of cost [also see Castrillon et al., 2023; Wiehler et al., 2022; Jamadar et al., 2024].
evidence: This is a speculative claim about metabolic markers of cost, supported by citations.

claim: Cognitive resources are limited.
source: Cognitive resources are limited.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cognitive science.

claim: Any unnecessary resource expenditure reduces cognitive and behavioral flexibility.
source: Therefore, any unnecessary resource expenditure reduces cognitive and behavioral flexibility (Friston, 2010; Shadmehr and Ahmed, 2020; Kahneman, 1973; Jamadar et al., 2024).
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of resource expenditure, supported by citations.

claim: The brain needs to distribute resources between cognitive operations and the oculomotor system.
source: As a result, the brain needs to distribute resources between cognitive operations and the oculomotor system.
evidence: This is an inference from the limited nature of cognitive resources.

claim: Resource distribution is adaptive to the general level of cognitive demand and available resources.
source: We found evidence for the idea that such resource distribution is adaptive to the general level of cognitive demand and available resources
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dual-task experiment findings.

claim: Higher cognitive demand is accompanied by smooth pursuits deviating more from to-be tracked targets.
source: For example, higher cognitive demand is accompanied by smooth pursuits deviating more from to-be tracked targets (Kosch et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on smooth pursuit and cognitive demand.

claim: Higher cognitive demand is accompanied by reduced (micro)saccade frequencies.
source: reduced (micro)saccade frequencies (Figure 4; Siegenthaler et al., 2014; May et al., 1990; Walter and Bex, 2021; Cui and Herrmann, 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and data from Figure 4.

claim: Higher cognitive demand is accompanied by slower peak saccade velocities.
source: and slower peak saccade velocities (Di Stasi et al., 2011; App and Debus, 1998; Sylvestre and Cullen, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccade velocity and cognitive demand.

claim: More precise saccades are accompanied with worse performance in a crowding task.
source: Relatedly, more precise saccades are accompanied with worse performance in a crowding task (Greenwood et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on saccade precision and crowding.

claim: Saccade costs are weighed against other cognitive operations such as using working memory.
source: Furthermore, it has been proposed that saccade costs are weighed against other cognitive operations such as using working memory (Somai et al., 2020; Van der Stigchel, 2020; Hoogerbrugge et al., 2023; Koevoet et al., 2023; Ballard et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on saccades and working memory.

claim: Saccades are thought to encode target objects in a mandatory fashion into (visual) working memory.
source: Saccades are thought to encode target objects in a mandatory fashion into (visual) working memory (Van der Stigchel and Hollingworth, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on saccades and working memory encoding.

claim: Cognitive resources are flexibly (dis)allocated to and from the oculomotor system based on the current demands to establish an optimal balance between performance and cost minimization.
source: Together, we propose that cognitive resources are flexibly (dis)allocated to and from the oculomotor system based on the current demands to establish an optimal balance between performance and cost minimization.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the findings from the dual-task experiment.

claim: Oculomotor control is generally thought to be steered by a network encompassing the frontal eye field, the supplementary eye field, the anterior cingulate cortex, the superior colliculus, and the cerebellum.
source: Although our data do not allow direct inferences about the precise neural circuitry underlying the computations of oculomotor selection, oculomotor control is generally thought to be steered by a network encompassing the frontal eye field (Paus, 1996; Bruce et al., 1985), the supplementary eye field (Schlag and Schlag-Rey, 1987; Amiez and Petrides, 2009; Sharika et al., 2013), the anterior cingulate cortex (Gaymard et al., 1998; Ruehl et al., 2021; Pouget, 2015; Conti and Irish, 2021), the superior colliculus (Gandhi and Katnani, 2011; Sparks, 1999; Sparks, 2002; Glimcher and Sparks, 1992; Wurtz and Albano, 1980; Basso and May, 2017; Strauch et al., 2022), and the cerebellum (Voogd and Barmack, 2006; Tanaka et al., 2021; Takagi et al., 1998; Van der Stigchel et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on oculomotor control networks.

claim: The areas involved in oculomotor control are all thought to be crucial for decision-making processes.
source: These areas are not just associated with oculomotor control, but are all also thought to be crucial for decision-making processes (Zhang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020; Basso and May, 2017; Jun et al., 2021; Crapse et al., 2018; Deverett et al., 2018; Basso et al., 2021; So and Stuphorn, 2016; Yang and Heinen, 2014; Chudasama et al., 2013; Baumann et al., 2015; Schall, 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research on these brain areas and decision-making.

claim: It is plausible that the weighing of saccade costs during saccade selection is performed by the oculomotor-decision making network.
source: It is plausible that the weighing of saccade costs during saccade selection is performed by this oculomotor-decision making network, but other areas such as orbitofrontal cortex may also play a role (Padoa-Schioppa and Conen, 2017; Wallis, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the neural basis of cost weighing, supported by citations.

claim: Only a cost account predicts a link between pupil size and saccade preferences.
source: Only a cost account predicts (1) a link between pupil size and saccade preferences
evidence: This is an argument for the cost account based on the pattern of findings.

claim: Only a cost account predicts a cardinal saccade bias.
source: (2) a cardinal saccade bias
evidence: This is an argument for the cost account based on the pattern of findings.

claim: Only a cost account predicts reduced saccade frequency under additional cognitive demand.
source: (3) reduced saccade frequency under additional cognitive demand
evidence: This is an argument for the cost account based on the pattern of findings.

claim: Only a cost account predicts disproportional cutting of especially those directions associated with more pupil dilation.
source: and (4) disproportional cutting of especially those directions associated with more pupil dilation.
evidence: This is an argument for the cost account based on the pattern of findings.

claim: The findings converge upon the conclusion that effort drives saccade selection.
source: Together, our findings converge upon the conclusion that effort drives saccade selection.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all findings in the study.

claim: Saccade selection is driven by physical properties of the environment, the observer's goals, selection history, and effort.
source: We propose that saccade selection is driven by physical properties of the environment, the observer's goals, selection history, and another fundamental factor: effort.
evidence: This is the main theoretical proposal of the paper, integrating effort with established factors.
